sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Bunjil** ​(*bunjil*) — ‌Creator Eaglehawk ‌· ​The eaglehawk ​who shaped ​the southeast ​— ​belongs to ‌the Aboriginal ​tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under the ‌domain ​"Creator Eaglehawk". ‌The name ​means ​"The eaglehawk"[^1].

​Bunjil is ​the ​**wedge-tailed eaglehawk ‌made ancestor** ​of the ‌Kulin ​nations of ‌central Victoria. ​In ‌the Dreaming ​he shaped ‌the ​mountains, rivers, ​plants, animals, ‌and the ‌laws ‌by which ​people should ​live. ‌He is ​one of ​two moiety ‌ancestors, ​paired with ​Waang the ‌crow, ​and after ‌his work ​on ​earth he ​was lifted ​into the ‌sky, ‌where he ​remains as ‌the ​star Altair.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly ‌spelling **Bunjil** ‌and serves ​its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/bunjil/). ​The ​displayed form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ​computed from ‌the displayed ​form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*bunjil* contains ‌the same ​letters: no ‌recovered ​diacritics or ‌special encoding ‌is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives ​for this ​name; ​**Bunjil** ​is a ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the ​name ‌means "The ​eaglehawk"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Bunjil** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. The ​plain ‌ASCII ​form *bunjil* ‌contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ​no ‌lost diacritics ‌or ‌encoding transition ​is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and provenance, ​and ​keep ​the original ‌evidence ‌visible. ​The displayed ‌form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ‌description computed ‌from ‌the ​displayed form ‌itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**b** ​→ **B** ​— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **u** ​→ ​**u** — ​Same
- ‌**n** ​→ **n** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**j** → ​**j** ‌— ‌Same
- **i** ​→ ​**i** ​— Same
- ​**l** ‌→ ‌**l** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The conventional ​scholarly reading of the ‌name is **/ˈbʊn.dʒɪl/** ‌— English transcription ​of the Kulin theonym.

​For the modern ​speaker, the closest approximation ​is: **'BUN-jil'** — ​stress the first ‌syllable, pronounce the 'j' ​as in 'jump', ​and keep the ‌final vowel short like ​the 'i' in ‌'kit'.

Because the ASCII ​form *bunjil* already ‌encodes the same ​conventional spelling, the restoration ​**Bunjil** does not ​add a stress mark, ​length mark, or ​distinctive letter. The ‌name keeps its restoration ​plain: the canonical ‌form is the ​preferred scholarly citation, while ‌the ASCII form ​is the lowercase ASCII ‌equivalent.

Because Bunjil ​belongs to an ‌oral tradition, the reconstructed ​pronunciation offered here ​is a scholarly romanization ‌rather than a ‌phonetic record of ‌a living speaker. The ​sounds of the ​original language include ‌phonemes that English does ​not distinguish, and ​early recorders used inconsistent ‌English-based spellings. PuniCodex ​therefore treats the ​capitalized scholarly form **Bunjil** ‌as the reference ​spelling, while noting that ‌the ASCII form ​represents the same ​romanized sequence. This is ​why the name ​is a plain restoration: ‌the restoration recovers ‌the proper-noun convention ​of the name without ‌adding a diacritic ​or special letter ​that the original ASCII ‌string could not ‌carry.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous writing ‌system ‌is securely ​attested ​for individual ​aboriginal ​names. ​The form ‌shown ​is a ​modern ‌scholarly transliteration.[^1]

​The ‌form **Bunjil** ​is ‌therefore a ​scholarly ​transliteration rather ​than ​an attested ​ancient ‌spelling; ​it encodes ‌the ​reconstructed sound ‌of ​the name ‌for ​modern use, ‌and ​no mark ​in ‌it is ‌decorative.

‌The Kulin ​languages ​were ‌traditionally oral, ​and ​Bunjil has ‌no ​original alphabetic ​script. ‌The name ​survives ‌in Latin ​transcription ​made by ​early ​settlers and ‌anthropologists. ‌PuniCodex ​treats **Bunjil** ‌as ​the scholarly ​citation ‌form; the ‌lowercase ‌form **bunjil** ‌differs ​only in ‌capitalization. ​The restoration ​adds ​only the ‌capital ​initial; ​the absence ​of ‌diacritics or ​special ​letters places ​the ‌name in ​a ‌plain restoration, ​not ‌because the ​figure ‌is less ‌significant, ​but ​because the ​ASCII ​form already ‌carries ‌the conventional ​spelling.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Bunjil's ​domain is ‌creation itself, ‌conceived ​not as ​a ​single moment ​but as ​an ‌ongoing relationship ​with Country. ​In ‌Kulin thought ​he ‌is the ​wedge-tailed eaglehawk ‌who ​shaped the ​physical world, ​established ​law, and ​then ‌took his ​place in ‌the ​sky as ‌a continuing ​watcher.

‌His influence ​extends ‌across several ​registers. As ​**Creator ‌of Country** ‌he is ‌responsible ​for landforms, ​water, ‌plants, and ​animals. As ​**Law-Giver** ‌he established ​the obligations ​that ‌bind people ​to ‌one another ​and to ​the ​land. As ​**Sky Ancestor** ‌he ‌provides a ​celestial ‌point of ​reference, identified ​with ‌the star ‌Altair. As ‌**Moiety ‌Founder** he ​heads ‌the eaglehawk ​half of ​the ​Kulin social ‌order, balanced ​by ​Waang the ​crow.

‌These domains ​are not ​abstract ​categories; they ‌are lived ​in ‌the seasonal ​calendar, ‌the songlines, ​the rock-art ‌site ‌of Bunjil's ​Shelter, and ​the ​contemporary cultural ​and ‌environmental work ‌of Kulin ​communities.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Bunjil's stories belong ​to the Dreaming of ‌the Kulin nations, especially ‌the Woiwurrung, Boonwurrung, and ​Wathaurong peoples. They explain ​how Country was made, ​how law was given, ​and how the creator ​withdrew into the sky ‌so that he might ​continue to watch over ​the world.[^1]

### Shaping the ‌Land and the Law ​(Creation)

In the Dreaming, ‌Bunjil travelled across what ​is now central Victoria. ‌He formed the mountains, ​traced the rivers, named ​the plants and animals, ​and laid down the ​laws that govern how ​people relate to one ‌another and to Country. These ​laws are not separate ‌from the land; they ​are remembered in place ‌names, songlines, and the ​seasonal responsibilities of each ‌clan. (Massola 1968; Howitt ​1904)[^2]

### The Sea That ‌Would Not Stop Rising ​(Deluge)

A Boonwurrung story ​tells of a time ‌when the Kulin nations ‌fell into conflict, neglecting ‌family and Country. The ​sea rose in anger ​and threatened to flood ‌the land. The people ​went to Bunjil and ​asked him to intervene. ‌Bunjil agreed, but only ​if the people would ​change their ways and ‌respect the law. He walked ​to the water's edge, ‌raised his spear, and ​commanded the sea to ​stop. It did. (Briggs, ​'Boon Wurrung Story')

### Lifted ​into the Sky (Ascent)

‌When his work on ‌earth was finished, Bunjil ​gathered his family and ‌asked Waang, who kept ​the winds in skin ​bags, to release enough ‌wind to carry them ‌to the sky. Waang ‌opened the whirlwind bag, ‌and the wind lifted ​Bunjil and his people ‌upward. Bunjil became the ​bright star Altair; his ​two wives, the black ​swans, became the stars ‌on either side. Some accounts ​say he left this ​world from the island ​of Deen Maar. (Howitt ‌1904; Mudrooroo 1994)

### Bunjil's ​Shelter (Sacred site)

In ​Gariwerd, the country now ​known as the Grampians, ‌Bunjil took shelter in ​a cave in the ‌Black Range. The rock-art ​site known as Bunjil's ‌Shelter is one of ​the most important Aboriginal ‌art places in Victoria ‌and remains under the ​care of Traditional Owners. ​It is not merely ​a memory of the ​ancestor; it is a ‌place where his presence ‌is understood to remain. ​(Parks Victoria 2009)

sources.citation: Massola, Aldo. Bunjil's Cave: Myths, Legends and Superstitions of the Aborigines of South-East Australia (Lansdowne Press, 1968).
Mudrooroo. Aboriginal Mythology: An A–Z (Thorsons, 1994).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Bunjil ​is not ‌a ‌solitary deity ​but ​one ​half of ​a ​Kulin social ‌and ​cosmological pair. ​The ‌eaglehawk moiety, ​headed ‌by ​Bunjil, is ‌balanced ​by the ​crow ​moiety, headed ​by ​Waang. This ‌pairing ​structures ‌kinship, marriage, ​and ‌ritual obligations ​across ‌the Kulin ​nations. ‌Different clans ​emphasise ​different ‌episodes — ‌the ‌Woiwurrung stress ​the ​sky ascent ‌and ​Altair, the ​Boonwurrung ‌remember ​the rising-sea ​story, ‌and the ​Wathaurong ‌preserve place-based ​accounts ​tied ​to the ​coast ‌and to ‌Bunjil's ​Shelter. In ‌the ​colonial period ​the ‌name ‌was recorded ‌under ‌many spellings ​— ‌Winjeel, Wingeel, ​Pundjel, ​Bunjel — ​reflecting ‌dialect ​variation and ​the ​difficulty of ‌rendering ​Aboriginal phonology ​in ​English orthography.[^1]

‌Kindred ​figures ‌in the ​PuniCodex ‌cross-tradition index ​include ‌[[ahuramazda|AhuraMazdā]], [[audhumla|Auðhumla]], ‌[[baiame|Baiame]], ​[[izanagi|Izanagi]], [[jagannatha|Jagannātha]], ​and ​[[oduduwa|Odùduwà]], ​each linked ‌through ‌creator / ​cosmogonic.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Bunjil ​teaches that ‌creation ‌is not ​a ​single event ​but ​a continuing ​responsibility. He ‌did ​not make ​the ‌land and ​depart; ‌he shaped ​it, ‌gave it ​law, ​and then ​withdrew ​into the ​sky ‌so that ​he could ‌go ​on watching. ‌The ​eaglehawk's eye ‌is ​still understood ‌to ​be turned ​toward ‌Country.

For ‌non-Indigenous ‌visitors, Bunjil ​is ​an invitation ‌to understand ​'Country' ​not as ‌real ​estate but ​as ‌a living ​inheritance ‌— a ​place ​that includes ​people, ​animals, plants, ‌water, sky, ‌and ​story, all ‌held ​together by ​obligations ‌that precede ‌the ‌colony by ‌tens ​of thousands ‌of ​years. The ​name ​Bunjil, even ‌in its ​simple ​Latin transcription, ​carries ‌that whole ​relationship. ​To restore ​the ‌capital is ​a ‌small act; ​to ‌remember what ​it ‌names is ‌the larger ​one ​— and ​the ​first of ‌the ‌obligations it ​describes.[^1]
